CHAPTER 16 - ELECTRICAL ENERGY

Introduction

Electricity is one of the most useful forms of energy. It lights our homes, runs fans and motors, heats water, and powers computers and phones. In this chapter we study the basic ideas needed to understand and use electricity: electric charge, electric current, potential difference, resistance, Ohm's law, combinations of resistors, electric power and energy, and the heating effect of current. We use plain ASCII for all formulae, for example V = I R.

16.1 ELECTRIC CHARGE

Matter is made of atoms, and atoms contain positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons. Electric charge is a basic property of these particles. There are two kinds of charge: positive and negative. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. The SI unit of charge is the COULOMB (C). The charge on one electron is e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C (negative), and the charge on one proton is +1.6 x 10^-19 C. A body becomes negatively charged when it gains electrons and positively charged when it loses electrons. Charge is conserved and is quantised, meaning any charge Q is a whole-number multiple of e: Q = n e, where n is an integer.

16.2 ELECTRIC CURRENT

When charges flow through a conductor we say an electric current flows. In metals the moving charges are free electrons. Electric current is the rate of flow of charge. If a charge Q flows past a point in a conductor in time t, then the current is

   I = Q / t

The SI unit of current is the AMPERE (A). One ampere is one coulomb of charge flowing per second: 1 A = 1 C / 1 s. Smaller units are the milliampere (1 mA = 10^-3 A) and microampere (1 microA = 10^-6 A). By convention, the direction of conventional current is taken as the direction in which positive charge would flow, that is, from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell through the external circuit. This is opposite to the actual direction of electron flow. Current is measured with an AMMETER, which is connected in SERIES in the circuit.

16.3 ELECTRIC POTENTIAL AND POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE

To make charge flow, we need a 'push'. This push is provided by a cell or battery, which maintains a potential difference between its terminals. Electric POTENTIAL at a point is the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point. The POTENTIAL DIFFERENCE (V) between two points is the work done (W) in moving a unit positive charge from one point to the other:

   V = W / Q

The SI unit of potential difference is the VOLT (V). One volt is one joule of work per coulomb of charge: 1 V = 1 J / 1 C. Potential difference is measured with a VOLTMETER, which is connected in PARALLEL across the two points. A cell or battery is the source of potential difference that drives current around a circuit.

16.4 ELECTRIC CIRCUIT AND CIRCUIT SYMBOLS

An electric circuit is a continuous closed conducting path along which an electric current can flow. A simple circuit contains a source (cell or battery), connecting wires, a switch (key), and a device such as a bulb or resistor. A circuit diagram represents these components using standard symbols: a cell is shown by a long thin line (positive) and a short thick line (negative); a battery is several cells in series; a switch is an open or closed gap; a resistor or rheostat by a rectangle; a bulb by a circle with a cross; an ammeter by a circle with 'A'; and a voltmeter by a circle with 'V'. When the switch is closed the path is complete and current flows; when it is open the circuit is broken and no current flows.

16.5 OHM'S LAW

In 1827 the German scientist G. S. Ohm investigated the relation between the potential difference across a conductor and the current through it. He found that, at constant temperature, the current I through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference V across its ends:

   V is proportional to I, so V = I R

where R is a constant for the given conductor at a given temperature, called its RESISTANCE. This is OHM'S LAW. If we plot a graph of V (on the y-axis) against I (on the x-axis) for a metallic conductor, we get a STRAIGHT LINE passing through the origin. The slope of the V-I graph equals the resistance R (slope = V / I = R). Conductors that obey Ohm's law are called ohmic; some devices (like a filament bulb at high temperature, or a diode) are non-ohmic and give curved V-I graphs.

16.6 RESISTANCE

RESISTANCE is the property of a conductor by which it opposes the flow of electric current through it. From Ohm's law, R = V / I. The SI unit of resistance is the OHM, with symbol the Greek letter omega (written here as 'ohm'). One ohm is the resistance of a conductor through which a current of 1 ampere flows when a potential difference of 1 volt is applied across it: 1 ohm = 1 V / 1 A. A good conductor has low resistance; an insulator has very high resistance. A component made to have a definite resistance is called a resistor. A variable resistor (RHEOSTAT) is used to change the current in a circuit.

16.7 FACTORS AFFECTING RESISTANCE AND RESISTIVITY

The resistance of a conductor (a wire) depends on four factors:
 (1) LENGTH (L): resistance is directly proportional to length. A longer wire has more resistance (R is proportional to L).
 (2) AREA OF CROSS-SECTION (A): resistance is inversely proportional to the area of cross-section. A thicker wire has less resistance (R is proportional to 1/A).
 (3) MATERIAL (nature of the conductor): different materials have different resistances even with the same dimensions.
 (4) TEMPERATURE: for metals, resistance increases as temperature rises.

Combining the first three factors:

   R = rho L / A

where rho (the Greek letter rho) is the RESISTIVITY (or specific resistance) of the material. Resistivity is a property of the material only, not of its shape. Its SI unit is the ohm metre (ohm m). Metals like silver and copper have very low resistivity (good conductors); alloys like nichrome have higher resistivity and are used in heating elements; insulators have very high resistivity. Rearranging, rho = R A / L.

16.8 COMBINATION OF RESISTANCES

Resistors can be joined in two basic ways: in series and in parallel.

SERIES COMBINATION: resistors are joined end to end so the SAME current flows through each. The potential difference of the source is shared among them. The equivalent (total) resistance is the sum of the individual resistances:

   R = R1 + R2 + R3

The equivalent resistance in series is always GREATER than the largest individual resistance. The current in a series circuit is the same everywhere.

PARALLEL COMBINATION: resistors are joined between the same two points, so the SAME potential difference acts across each, while the current divides among them. The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances:

   1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3

The equivalent resistance in parallel is always LESS than the smallest individual resistance. Household wiring uses parallel connections so that each appliance gets the full supply voltage and can be switched on or off independently.

16.9 ELECTRIC POWER

ELECTRIC POWER is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or supplied in a circuit. If a potential difference V drives a current I, then the power is

   P = V I

Using Ohm's law (V = I R) we can write this in three equivalent forms:

   P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R

The SI unit of power is the WATT (W). One watt is one joule per second: 1 W = 1 J / 1 s. It is also equal to one volt-ampere: 1 W = 1 V x 1 A. A larger unit is the kilowatt (1 kW = 1000 W). The power rating marked on an appliance, e.g. '60 W, 220 V', tells us the power it consumes at the rated voltage.

16.10 HEATING EFFECT OF CURRENT AND JOULE'S LAW

When current flows through a resistor, the electrical energy is converted into heat. This is the HEATING EFFECT of current. The free electrons collide with the atoms of the conductor and lose energy, which appears as heat. James Prescott Joule studied this and gave JOULE'S LAW OF HEATING: the heat H produced in a resistor is

   H = I^2 R t

That is, the heat produced is directly proportional to (i) the square of the current (I^2), (ii) the resistance R, and (iii) the time t for which the current flows. Since P = I^2 R, we can also write H = P t. The heat is measured in joules when I is in amperes, R in ohms and t in seconds.

16.11 APPLICATIONS OF THE HEATING EFFECT

The heating effect of current is used in many devices:
 - ELECTRIC HEATER, IRON, GEYSER, TOASTER: a coil of high-resistance alloy (nichrome) gets hot when current passes through it. Nichrome is used because it has high resistivity and does not oxidise (burn) readily at high temperature.
 - ELECTRIC BULB (incandescent): a thin tungsten filament becomes white hot and glows, giving light. Tungsten is used for its very high melting point. The bulb is filled with inert gas to prevent the filament from burning.
 - ELECTRIC FUSE: a short piece of wire of low melting point placed in series in a circuit. If the current becomes too large (due to overload or short circuit), the heat produced melts the fuse wire and breaks the circuit, protecting appliances and preventing fire.

16.12 ELECTRICAL ENERGY AND ITS COMMERCIAL UNIT

Electrical ENERGY consumed is the product of power and time:

   E = P t = V I t

In SI units, energy is measured in joules (J) when P is in watts and t in seconds. But the joule is a small unit for household use. The COMMERCIAL UNIT of electrical energy is the KILOWATT-HOUR (kWh), also called 'one unit' of electricity. One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed when an appliance of power 1 kilowatt is used for 1 hour:

   1 kWh = 1 kW x 1 h = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J

Electricity bills are charged in kilowatt-hours (units). To find the energy in kWh: energy (kWh) = power (kW) x time (h).

16.13 WORKED NUMERICALS

Example 1 (Ohm's law): A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a resistor and a current of 2 A flows. Find R. Solution: R = V / I = 12 / 2 = 6 ohm.

Example 2 (series): Three resistors 2 ohm, 3 ohm and 5 ohm are joined in series. Equivalent resistance R = 2 + 3 + 5 = 10 ohm.

Example 3 (parallel): Two resistors 6 ohm and 3 ohm are in parallel. 1/R = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6, so R = 2 ohm.

Example 4 (power): A bulb is rated 60 W at 220 V. Current I = P / V = 60 / 220 = 0.27 A. Its resistance R = V^2 / P = (220)^2 / 60 = 48400 / 60 = 807 ohm (approx).

Example 5 (Joule heating): A current of 3 A flows through a 4 ohm resistor for 5 s. Heat produced H = I^2 R t = 3^2 x 4 x 5 = 9 x 4 x 5 = 180 J.

Example 6 (energy / kWh): An electric heater of 2 kW is used for 3 hours per day. Energy per day = 2 x 3 = 6 kWh (6 units). If 1 unit costs 5 rupees, the cost per day = 6 x 5 = 30 rupees.

SUMMARY

- Electric charge is measured in coulombs; charge on an electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
- Electric current I = Q / t; SI unit ampere (A); measured by an ammeter in series.
- Potential difference V = W / Q; SI unit volt (V); measured by a voltmeter in parallel.
- Ohm's law: V = I R (constant temperature); the V-I graph is a straight line through the origin.
- Resistance R = V / I; SI unit ohm. R depends on length, area, material and temperature: R = rho L / A.
- Series: R = R1 + R2 + R3 (same current). Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 (same voltage).
- Electric power P = V I = I^2 R = V^2 / R; SI unit watt (W).
- Heating effect: Joule's law H = I^2 R t. Used in heaters, bulbs and fuses.
- Electrical energy E = P t; commercial unit is the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

sections.heading: Electric charge, current and potential difference
bullets: Electric charge is a basic property of matter; the SI unit is the coulomb (C). The charge on an electron is 1.6 x 10^-19 C.
Electric current is the rate of flow of charge: I = Q/t. The SI unit is the ampere (A); 1 A = 1 C/s. An ammeter is connected in series.
Conventional current flows from the positive to the negative terminal through the external circuit - opposite to electron flow.
Potential difference V = W/Q is the work done per unit charge; SI unit volt (V), 1 V = 1 J/C. A voltmeter is connected in parallel.

sections.heading: Ohm's law and resistance
bullets: Ohm's law: at constant temperature, V = I R, so current is directly proportional to potential difference.
The V-I graph of an ohmic conductor is a straight line through the origin; its slope equals the resistance R.
Resistance R = V/I opposes the flow of current; the SI unit is the ohm. A resistor has a fixed resistance; a rheostat is a variable resistor.

sections.heading: Factors affecting resistance and resistivity
bullets: Resistance increases with length (R proportional to L) and decreases with cross-sectional area (R proportional to 1/A).
Resistance depends on the material and on temperature; for metals resistance rises with temperature.
R = rho L / A, where rho is resistivity (unit ohm metre), a property of the material only. Metals have low rho; alloys like nichrome higher.

sections.heading: Series and parallel combinations
bullets: In series the same current flows through each resistor and the equivalent resistance is R = R1 + R2 + R3 (greater than the largest).
In parallel the same voltage acts across each resistor and 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 (less than the smallest).
Household appliances are connected in parallel so each gets the full supply voltage and can be switched independently.

sections.heading: Power, energy and the heating effect
bullets: Electric power P = V I = I^2 R = V^2/R; SI unit watt (W), 1 W = 1 J/s.
Electrical energy E = P t; the commercial unit is the kilowatt-hour: 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J (one 'unit' of electricity).
Joule's law of heating: H = I^2 R t. This heating effect is used in heaters and bulbs (nichrome, tungsten) and in the fuse for safety.

key_takeaways: Electric current I = Q/t is measured in amperes; potential difference V = W/Q is measured in volts.
Ohm's law V = I R holds at constant temperature; the V-I graph is a straight line whose slope is the resistance.
Resistance R = rho L / A depends on length, cross-sectional area, material and temperature.
Series resistance adds (R = R1 + R2 + R3); parallel resistance combines as 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.
Electric power P = V I = I^2 R = V^2/R; the SI unit is the watt.
Electrical energy E = P t is sold in kilowatt-hours; 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
Joule's law H = I^2 R t describes the heating effect used in heaters, bulbs and fuses.

The rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, I = Q/t. SI unit: ampere (A).
The SI unit of electric current; one ampere is one coulomb of charge flowing per second (1 A = 1 C/s).
The work done in moving a unit positive charge between two points, V = W/Q. SI unit: volt (V).
The SI unit of potential difference; 1 volt = 1 joule per coulomb (1 V = 1 J/C).

The opposition of a conductor to the flow of current, R = V/I. SI unit: ohm.
The SI unit of resistance; 1 ohm is the resistance when 1 volt drives 1 ampere (1 ohm = 1 V/A).
A property of a material giving its resistance per unit length and area, rho = R A / L. SI unit: ohm metre.
Resistors joined end to end carrying the same current; equivalent resistance R = R1 + R2 + R3.
Resistors joined across the same two points with the same voltage; 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3.
The rate of consuming electrical energy, P = V I = I^2 R = V^2/R. SI unit: watt (W).
The commercial unit of electrical energy ('one unit'); 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
The heat produced in a resistor H = I^2 R t, proportional to I squared, to R and to time t.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Electrical Energy (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science and Technology (212) worksheet for Lesson 16. Attempt all questions. Show working for numerical problems and state the units in your answers.

questions.question: Define electric current and state its SI unit. A charge of 60 C flows through a wire in 30 s. Find the current.
questions.answer:
Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor: I = Q/t. Its SI unit is the ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 C/s.
Given Q = 60 C, t = 30 s: I = Q/t = 60/30 = 2 A.
questions.explanation: Definition + direct application of I = Q/t.

questions.question: State Ohm's law. Draw (describe) the V-I graph for a metallic conductor and state what its slope represents.
questions.answer:
Ohm's law: at constant temperature, the current I through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference V across its ends, so V = I R, where R is the resistance.
The V-I graph (V on the y-axis, I on the x-axis) is a STRAIGHT LINE passing through the origin. The slope of this line equals the resistance R of the conductor (slope = V/I = R).
questions.explanation: Statement of the law and interpretation of the linear V-I graph.

questions.question: List the four factors on which the resistance of a wire depends, and write the relation R = rho L / A explaining each symbol.
questions.answer:
Resistance of a wire depends on: (1) length L - R increases with length; (2) area of cross-section A - R decreases as A increases; (3) the material of the wire; (4) temperature - for metals R rises with temperature.
The relation is R = rho L / A, where R = resistance (ohm), rho = resistivity of the material (ohm metre), L = length (m) and A = area of cross-section (m^2). Resistivity rho depends only on the material, not on its shape.
questions.explanation: Four factors plus the resistivity relation.

questions.question: Three resistors of 4 ohm, 6 ohm and 12 ohm are connected (a) in series and (b) in parallel. Calculate the equivalent resistance in each case.
questions.answer:
(a) Series: R = R1 + R2 + R3 = 4 + 6 + 12 = 22 ohm.
(b) Parallel: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/6 + 1/12. Take LCM 12: 1/R = 3/12 + 2/12 + 1/12 = 6/12 = 1/2. So R = 2 ohm.
Note the series value (22 ohm) is greater than the largest resistor, while the parallel value (2 ohm) is less than the smallest resistor.
questions.explanation: Apply series and parallel formulae and compare results.

questions.question: An electric bulb is rated 100 W at 220 V. Find (a) the current it draws, (b) its resistance, and (c) the energy in kWh it consumes if used for 5 hours.
questions.answer:
(a) Current I = P/V = 100/220 = 0.45 A (approx).
(b) Resistance R = V^2 / P = (220)^2 / 100 = 48400 / 100 = 484 ohm.
(c) Energy = power x time = 0.1 kW x 5 h = 0.5 kWh (0.5 unit).
questions.explanation: Uses P = V I, R = V^2/P and E = P t in kWh.

questions.question: State Joule's law of heating. A current of 2 A flows through a resistor of 10 ohm for 30 s. Calculate the heat produced.
questions.answer:
Joule's law of heating: the heat produced in a resistor is H = I^2 R t, i.e. it is proportional to the square of the current, to the resistance, and to the time.
Given I = 2 A, R = 10 ohm, t = 30 s: H = I^2 R t = (2)^2 x 10 x 30 = 4 x 10 x 30 = 1200 J.
questions.explanation: Statement plus substitution into H = I^2 R t.

questions.question: Why is nichrome used as the heating element in electric heaters, and why is tungsten used for bulb filaments?
questions.answer:
Nichrome is used in heaters because it has a HIGH RESISTIVITY (so it produces a lot of heat for the current passing through it) and it does not oxidise or burn readily even at high temperatures, so the element lasts long.
Tungsten is used for bulb filaments because it has a VERY HIGH MELTING POINT, so it can be heated to a white-hot temperature and glow brightly without melting. The bulb is filled with an inert gas to stop the filament from burning away.
questions.explanation: Material properties: high resistivity (nichrome), high melting point (tungsten).

questions.question: What is an electric fuse? Explain how it protects an electric circuit.
questions.answer:
An electric fuse is a short piece of wire of low melting point connected in SERIES in a circuit. Under normal conditions the rated current passes through it harmlessly.
If the current becomes too large (because of an overload or a short circuit), the heat produced (H = I^2 R t) melts the fuse wire. This breaks the circuit and stops the current, protecting the appliances from damage and preventing fire.
questions.explanation: Fuse definition and protective action via the heating effect.

questions.question: How is an ammeter connected in a circuit, and how is a voltmeter connected? State the SI units they measure.
questions.answer:
An AMMETER measures electric current and is connected in SERIES in the circuit, so that the whole current to be measured passes through it. It reads current in amperes (A).
A VOLTMETER measures potential difference and is connected in PARALLEL across the two points (or component) whose potential difference is to be measured. It reads in volts (V).
questions.explanation: Ammeter in series (amperes); voltmeter in parallel (volts).

questions.question: A potential difference of 12 V is applied across a resistor and a current of 0.5 A flows. (a) Find the resistance. (b) Find the power dissipated. (c) Find the energy consumed in 10 minutes (in joules).
questions.answer:
(a) Resistance R = V/I = 12/0.5 = 24 ohm.
(b) Power P = V I = 12 x 0.5 = 6 W.
(c) Time t = 10 minutes = 600 s. Energy E = P t = 6 x 600 = 3600 J.
questions.explanation: Combines Ohm's law, power P = V I and energy E = P t.

questions.question: Define electric current and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, I = Q/t. Its SI unit is the ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 coulomb per second.

questions.question: Define potential difference and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Potential difference between two points is the work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point to the other, V = W/Q. Its SI unit is the volt (V), where 1 V = 1 joule per coulomb.

questions.question: What is conventional current and how does its direction compare with electron flow?
questions.answer: Conventional current is the direction in which positive charge would flow, taken from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell through the external circuit. In a metal the actual moving charges are electrons, which flow in the OPPOSITE direction (from negative to positive). So conventional current is opposite to electron flow.

questions.question: How are an ammeter and a voltmeter connected in a circuit?
questions.answer: An ammeter measures current and is connected in SERIES, so the whole current passes through it. A voltmeter measures potential difference and is connected in PARALLEL across the component whose PD is to be measured.

questions.question: A charge of 90 C passes through a wire in 30 s. Calculate the current.
questions.answer: I = Q/t = 90/30 = 3 A. The current in the wire is 3 amperes.

questions.question: A current of 0.4 A flows in a circuit for 2 minutes. Find the total charge that flows.
questions.answer: Time t = 2 minutes = 120 s. Charge Q = I t = 0.4 x 120 = 48 C. So 48 coulombs of charge flow.
questions.explanation: Convert minutes to seconds; Q = I t.

questions.question: How much work is done in moving a charge of 4 C through a potential difference of 6 V?
questions.answer: Work W = V Q = 6 x 4 = 24 J. So 24 joules of work is done.

questions.question: State Ohm's law.
questions.answer: Ohm's law states that, at constant temperature, the electric current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference applied across its ends. Hence V = I R, where R is the constant resistance of the conductor.

questions.question: A resistor carries a current of 0.25 A when 5 V is applied. Find its resistance.
questions.answer: R = V/I = 5/0.25 = 20 ohm. The resistance is 20 ohms.

questions.question: What does the V-I graph of a metallic conductor look like, and what does its slope represent?
questions.answer: For a metallic (ohmic) conductor at constant temperature, the V-I graph (V on the y-axis, I on the x-axis) is a STRAIGHT LINE passing through the origin. This shows V is directly proportional to I. The SLOPE of the line equals V/I, which is the RESISTANCE R of the conductor. A steeper line means a larger resistance.

questions.question: The current through a resistor is 2 A at 4 V. Predict the current if the voltage is raised to 10 V (temperature unchanged).
questions.answer: First find the resistance: R = V/I = 4/2 = 2 ohm (constant, since temperature is unchanged). At 10 V, the current I = V/R = 10/2 = 5 A. So the current rises to 5 A. This works because, by Ohm's law, current is directly proportional to voltage for an ohmic resistor.
questions.explanation: Find R then re-apply Ohm's law.

questions.question: Define resistance and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Resistance is the property of a conductor by which it opposes the flow of electric current through it, R = V/I. Its SI unit is the ohm; 1 ohm is the resistance when a PD of 1 V drives a current of 1 A.

questions.question: List the factors on which the resistance of a wire depends.
questions.answer: The resistance of a wire depends on: (1) its LENGTH - R increases with length; (2) its AREA OF CROSS-SECTION - R decreases as area increases; (3) the MATERIAL of the wire (its resistivity); and (4) its TEMPERATURE - for metals R increases as temperature rises.

questions.question: Define resistivity and write the relation linking resistance to resistivity.
questions.answer: Resistivity (rho) is the resistance offered by a unit cube (unit length and unit area) of a material; it depends only on the material and its temperature, not on its shape. The relation is R = rho L / A, where L is the length and A is the area of cross-section. The SI unit of resistivity is the ohm metre (ohm m).

questions.question: A wire has resistance 10 ohm. If a second wire of the same material has twice the length and twice the area of cross-section, find its resistance.
questions.answer: R = rho L / A. For the second wire, length is 2L and area is 2A, so R2 = rho (2L)/(2A) = rho L / A = R1 = 10 ohm. The doubling of length and area cancel out, so the resistance is unchanged at 10 ohm.

questions.question: Write the formula for the equivalent resistance of resistors in series and in parallel.
questions.answer: Series: R = R1 + R2 + R3 (resistances add). Parallel: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 (reciprocals add).

questions.question: Find the equivalent resistance of 5 ohm, 10 ohm and 15 ohm connected in series.
questions.answer: In series the resistances add: R = 5 + 10 + 15 = 30 ohm.

questions.question: Find the equivalent resistance of two resistors 4 ohm and 12 ohm connected in parallel.
questions.answer: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/12. Taking LCM 12: 1/R = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3. So R = 3 ohm. The parallel value (3 ohm) is less than the smaller resistor (4 ohm), as expected.

questions.question: Why are domestic appliances connected in parallel and not in series?
questions.answer: Appliances are connected in parallel so that (1) each receives the FULL supply voltage and works at its rated power, and (2) each can be switched ON or OFF independently without affecting the others. In series, all would share the voltage and a break anywhere would stop every appliance.

questions.question: A 2 ohm and a 3 ohm resistor are in series; this combination is in parallel with a 5 ohm resistor. Find the total resistance.
questions.answer: Series part: 2 + 3 = 5 ohm. This 5 ohm is in parallel with 5 ohm: 1/R = 1/5 + 1/5 = 2/5, so R = 5/2 = 2.5 ohm. The total resistance is 2.5 ohm.

questions.question: Define electric power and state its SI unit.
questions.answer: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed or supplied in a circuit, P = V I = I^2 R = V^2/R. Its SI unit is the watt (W), where 1 W = 1 joule per second.

questions.question: An electric iron draws 5 A at 220 V. Calculate its power.
questions.answer: P = V I = 220 x 5 = 1100 W = 1.1 kW. The power of the iron is 1100 watts.

questions.question: A bulb is marked 60 W, 220 V. Find its resistance and the current it draws at the rated voltage.
questions.answer: Resistance R = V^2 / P = (220)^2 / 60 = 48400 / 60 = 807 ohm (approx). Current I = P/V = 60/220 = 0.27 A (approx). So R is about 807 ohm and I about 0.27 A.

questions.question: Two bulbs are rated 40 W and 100 W for the same voltage. Which has the greater resistance? Explain.
questions.answer: For the same voltage V, power P = V^2 / R, so R = V^2 / P. Resistance is INVERSELY proportional to power. The 40 W bulb has the lower power, so it has the GREATER resistance. The 100 W bulb has the lower resistance and draws more current.
questions.explanation: R = V^2/P; lower power means higher R.

questions.question: What is one kilowatt-hour and how is it related to the joule?
questions.answer: One kilowatt-hour (kWh) is the electrical energy consumed when an appliance of power 1 kilowatt is used for 1 hour. It is the commercial unit of electrical energy ('one unit'). In joules: 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J.

questions.question: Calculate the energy consumed (in kWh) by a 1.5 kW heater used for 4 hours.
questions.answer: Energy = power x time = 1.5 kW x 4 h = 6 kWh. So the heater consumes 6 units of electrical energy.

questions.question: A household uses five 100 W bulbs for 5 hours daily. If 1 unit costs 5 rupees, find the monthly (30 day) cost.
questions.answer: Power of 5 bulbs = 5 x 100 = 500 W = 0.5 kW. Daily energy = 0.5 kW x 5 h = 2.5 kWh. Monthly energy = 2.5 x 30 = 75 kWh. Cost = 75 x 5 = 375 rupees.
questions.explanation: Total power, daily then monthly energy, then cost.

questions.question: State Joule's law of heating.
questions.answer: Joule's law of heating states that the heat H produced in a resistor is H = I^2 R t, i.e. it is directly proportional to (i) the square of the current I, (ii) the resistance R, and (iii) the time t for which the current flows.
questions.explanation: Statement of H = I^2 R t.

questions.question: A current of 5 A flows through a 4 ohm resistor for 10 s. Find the heat produced.
questions.answer: H = I^2 R t = (5)^2 x 4 x 10 = 25 x 4 x 10 = 1000 J. The heat produced is 1000 joules.

questions.question: Explain how an electric fuse protects a circuit and why it is made of a low-melting-point material.
questions.answer: A fuse is a short wire of low melting point connected in SERIES with the circuit. Normally the rated current flows through it safely. If the current rises too high (overload or short circuit), the heat produced (H = I^2 R t) raises the fuse wire's temperature above its melting point, so it MELTS and breaks the circuit. This stops the excess current and protects appliances and prevents fire. A low-melting-point material is used so that it melts quickly at a safe current limit before the wiring or appliances are damaged.
questions.explanation: Series fuse melts on overload; low melting point for quick action.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A student connects a cell, an ammeter, a resistor and a key in a circuit. When the key is closed, the ammeter reads 0.6 A and a stopwatch shows the current flows for 50 s.

(i) Define electric current.
(ii) How is the ammeter connected?
(iii) Calculate the charge that flows in 50 s.
(iv) State the SI unit of charge.
questions.answer:
(i) Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge, I = Q/t.
(ii) The ammeter is connected in SERIES so the full current passes through it.
(iii) Q = I t = 0.6 x 50 = 30 C.
(iv) The SI unit of charge is the coulomb (C).
questions.explanation: Definition, ammeter connection, Q = I t, unit.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

In an experiment, the potential difference V across a resistor was varied and the current I measured. The readings gave a straight-line V-I graph through the origin, and for one reading V = 6 V with I = 1.5 A.

(i) What law does the straight-line graph confirm?
(ii) What does the slope of the V-I graph represent?
(iii) Calculate the resistance of the resistor.
(iv) Is this conductor ohmic or non-ohmic?
questions.answer:
(i) It confirms Ohm's law (V is proportional to I at constant temperature).
(ii) The slope of the V-I graph represents the resistance R.
(iii) R = V/I = 6/1.5 = 4 ohm.
(iv) Since the graph is a straight line through the origin, the conductor is OHMIC.
questions.explanation: Ohm's law, slope = R, compute R, ohmic.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The resistance of a metal wire depends on its length, its area of cross-section, the material it is made of, and its temperature. The resistivity rho is a property of the material.

(i) Write the relation between R, rho, L and A.
(ii) How does resistance change if length is doubled (area fixed)?
(iii) How does resistance change if the area is doubled (length fixed)?
(iv) Name one material with high resistivity used for heaters.
questions.answer:
(i) R = rho L / A.
(ii) Doubling the length doubles the resistance (R is proportional to L).
(iii) Doubling the area halves the resistance (R is proportional to 1/A).
(iv) Nichrome (a high-resistivity alloy) is used for heater elements.
questions.explanation: Relation and effects of length and area; nichrome.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Three resistors of 2 ohm, 4 ohm and 4 ohm are available. A student connects all three first in series and then all three in parallel across a 12 V battery.

(i) Find the equivalent resistance in series.
(ii) Find the current drawn from the battery in the series case.
(iii) Find the equivalent resistance in parallel.
(iv) Which arrangement draws more current from the battery?
questions.answer:
(i) Series: R = 2 + 4 + 4 = 10 ohm.
(ii) Current = V/R = 12/10 = 1.2 A.
(iii) Parallel: 1/R = 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 4/4 = 1, so R = 1 ohm.
(iv) The PARALLEL arrangement has lower resistance (1 ohm), so it draws more current (12/1 = 12 A) than the series arrangement.
questions.explanation: Series and parallel equivalents and currents.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A circuit has a 6 ohm resistor in series with a parallel combination of two 4 ohm resistors. The supply is 10 V.

(i) Find the resistance of the parallel pair.
(ii) Find the total resistance of the circuit.
(iii) Find the current drawn from the supply.
(iv) State the quantity that is the same across the two parallel resistors.
questions.answer:
(i) Parallel pair: 1/R = 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 1/2, so R = 2 ohm.
(ii) Total = 6 + 2 = 8 ohm (series).
(iii) Current I = V/R = 10/8 = 1.25 A.
(iv) The potential difference (voltage) is the same across the two parallel resistors.
questions.explanation: Combine parallel then series; compute current.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

An electric motor operates at 220 V and draws a current of 4 A.

(i) Write the formula for electric power.
(ii) Calculate the power of the motor.
(iii) State the SI unit of power.
(iv) Express the power in kilowatts.
questions.answer:
(i) P = V I (also I^2 R or V^2/R).
(ii) P = V I = 220 x 4 = 880 W.
(iii) The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
(iv) 880 W = 0.88 kW.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A heater of resistance 25 ohm is connected to a 250 V supply.

(i) Find the current through the heater.
(ii) Find the power of the heater using P = V I.
(iii) Verify the power using P = V^2/R.
(iv) State the SI unit of electric power.
questions.answer:
(i) I = V/R = 250/25 = 10 A.
(ii) P = V I = 250 x 10 = 2500 W.
(iii) P = V^2/R = (250)^2/25 = 62500/25 = 2500 W (same value).
(iv) The SI unit of power is the watt (W).

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A family uses a 2 kW geyser for 1 hour, a 1 kW iron for 2 hours and ten 100 W bulbs for 5 hours each day. Electricity costs 6 rupees per unit.

(i) Find the energy used by the geyser per day.
(ii) Find the energy used by the iron per day.
(iii) Find the total energy used by the bulbs per day.
(iv) Find the total daily cost.
questions.answer:
(i) Geyser: 2 kW x 1 h = 2 kWh.
(ii) Iron: 1 kW x 2 h = 2 kWh.
(iii) Bulbs: total power = 10 x 100 = 1000 W = 1 kW; energy = 1 kW x 5 h = 5 kWh.
(iv) Total daily energy = 2 + 2 + 5 = 9 kWh. Cost = 9 x 6 = 54 rupees.
questions.explanation: Energy per appliance in kWh, then total cost.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The commercial unit of electrical energy is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), also called a 'unit'. Electricity bills are charged per unit consumed.

(i) Define one kilowatt-hour.
(ii) Convert 1 kWh into joules.
(iii) How many units does a 1000 W appliance use in 3 hours?
(iv) Why is the kWh preferred over the joule for billing?
questions.answer:
(i) One kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a 1 kW appliance running for 1 hour.
(ii) 1 kWh = 1000 W x 3600 s = 3.6 x 10^6 J.
(iii) Energy = 1 kW x 3 h = 3 kWh = 3 units.
(iv) The joule is a very small unit, so the energy used by households would be a huge number of joules. The kWh gives convenient, manageable numbers for billing.
questions.explanation: Definition, conversion, units used, why kWh.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

When current passes through a resistor, electrical energy is converted into heat. This heating effect is used in heaters, bulbs and protective fuses.

(i) State Joule's law of heating.
(ii) A 10 ohm resistor carries 3 A for 20 s; find the heat produced.
(iii) Why is tungsten used for bulb filaments?
(iv) How does a fuse protect a circuit?
questions.answer:
(i) Joule's law: H = I^2 R t.
(ii) H = I^2 R t = (3)^2 x 10 x 20 = 9 x 10 x 20 = 1800 J.
(iii) Tungsten is used because it has a very high melting point, so it can glow white-hot to give light without melting.
(iv) A fuse is a low-melting-point wire in series; if the current is too high it melts (due to I^2 R t heating) and breaks the circuit, protecting appliances and preventing fire.
questions.explanation: Joule's law, calculation, tungsten, fuse action.
